statement: Many species (most animals and plants) have an embryo stage that does not feed.

scores.rationale: The corpus provides strong, consistent support for the stylized fact that most animals (and many plants) have a non-feeding embryo stage. Numerous DEB-theory snippets explicitly define the embryo as the life stage that does not feed and relies on maternal/egg reserves (snippets 4, 5, 8, 11, 12, 13, 14, 17). Several snippets extend the principle to foetal development (mammals, velvet worms) and plants, framing foetuses energetically as embryos because they do not take food (snippets 2, 9, 10, 15), and note edge cases like lecithotrophic larvae and aphids that are handled within the same conceptual framework (snippets 3, 6, 16) without contradicting the fact. No snippet contradicts the claim; snippets 1, 7, and 18 are topically related to feeding/reproduction but do not directly bear on the embryo-non-feeding statement. Overall consensus clearly corroborates the fact.

scores.rationale: The stylized fact—that embryos of most animals and plants do not feed but rely on maternal nutrient provisioning—is indirectly but consistently supported by several snippets. Snippets 7 and 12 describe maternal/seed structures (endosperm, seed coat, pericarp) nurturing plant embryos, and snippet 12 explicitly parallels mammalian placental nutrient translocation, both implying the embryo is provisioned rather than self-feeding. Snippets 10 and 11 (Quiet Embryo Hypothesis) describe preimplantation embryos relying on metabolite turnover from maternal supply rather than external feeding. Snippet 9 references non-feeding life stages provisioned by reserves. No snippet contradicts the fact. However, none directly state 'embryos do not feed' as a comparative cross-taxa generalization, so support is moderate and circumstantial rather than strong, leaving the corpus corroborating in direction but limited in evidentiary force.
